choices.explanation: DynamoDB global tables use multi-active (not primary-replica) replication; every replica table accepts writes. Routing `eu-west-1` Lambda writes to `us-east-1` reintroduces a cross-Region write dependency and defeats the purpose of the global table.

choices.text: The command creates a DynamoDB global table with active-active replication. No further changes are needed because API Gateway automatically routes all requests to the nearest regional DynamoDB endpoint based on the Route 53 latency routing policy already in place.
choices.explanation: API Gateway and Route 53 latency routing operate at the HTTP request layer; they do not control which DynamoDB endpoint the Lambda function code connects to. Lambda must explicitly be configured to use the local regional endpoint.

choices.text: The command creates a DynamoDB global table that replicates data to `eu-west-1` with eventual consistency. To eliminate the single point of failure, the Lambda functions should use DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in each Region as a caching layer to absorb read traffic in the event of a DynamoDB outage.
choices.explanation: DAX is an in-memory write-through cache and does not serve as a failover for DynamoDB; if the underlying DynamoDB table is unavailable, DAX write-through operations also fail. DAX does not mitigate a Regional DynamoDB outage.

questions.tip: Consider what global tables provide at the replication layer, and which component in the application code still needs to be updated to use the nearest replica.
questions.explanation:
DynamoDB global tables provide multi-active replication, meaning every regional replica accepts reads and writes independently. The remaining gap is in the application layer: Lambda functions must target the local regional DynamoDB endpoint to truly eliminate the cross-Region dependency.

**Why it works:** `create-global-table` with replicas in both Regions establishes synchronous propagation of writes across replicas. When Lambda in `eu-west-1` connects to `dynamodb.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com`, it reads and writes locally with no dependency on `us-east-1`. Combined with Route 53 latency routing, the architecture is fully multi-active.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Option B: Global tables are multi-active, not primary-replica. Routing `eu-west-1` writes to `us-east-1` reintroduces the cross-Region dependency that caused the original incident.
- Option C: Route 53 and API Gateway routing do not influence which DynamoDB endpoint is used inside Lambda function code; the SDK endpoint must be explicitly configured.
- Option D: DAX is a write-through cache, not a standalone datastore. It does not protect against a DynamoDB regional failure because all write operations pass through to DynamoDB.

skills: 2.2.4: Implementing designs to mitigate single points of failure.
questions.question:
The organization is migrating a monolithic e-commerce application to AWS. The architecture review board has identified three single points of failure in the proposed design: the web tier has all instances in a single Availability Zone, the RDS database has no standby, and the session cache uses a single ElastiCache node. The team must remediate all three single points of failure within the existing VPC, which has public and private subnets in `us-east-1a`, `us-east-1b`, and `us-east-1c`.

Which TWO changes will MOST effectively eliminate the identified single points of failure with the least operational overhead?

choices.text: Update the EC2 Auto Scaling group to specify all three private subnet IDs across `us-east-1a`, `us-east-1b`, and `us-east-1c` using `--vpc-zone-identifier`, set the minimum capacity to 3, and register the Auto Scaling group with the Application Load Balancer target group across all three AZs.
choices.explanation: Distributing the Auto Scaling group across three AZs using `--vpc-zone-identifier` with all three subnet IDs ensures the web tier survives the loss of any single AZ. The ALB already spans multiple AZs and will route only to healthy targets.

choices.text: Enable Multi-AZ on the RDS instance via the `--multi-az` parameter and replace the single-node ElastiCache cluster with an ElastiCache for Redis replication group using `--automatic-failover-enabled` and replicas in at least two AZs.
choices.explanation: RDS Multi-AZ provides synchronous standby replication with automatic DNS failover, and ElastiCache for Redis with automatic failover and multi-AZ replicas eliminates both the database and session cache single points of failure in a single change each, with AWS managing failover automatically.

choices.text: Create manual RDS snapshots every 30 minutes using an AWS Lambda function triggered by EventBridge Scheduler, and store the snapshots in Amazon S3 with cross-Region replication enabled to `us-west-2` for disaster recovery.
choices.explanation: Manual snapshots provide point-in-time recovery but require manual restoration effort and do not eliminate the single-AZ RDS instance as a single point of failure. Automated failover via Multi-AZ is the correct mechanism for high availability.

choices.text: Deploy a second EC2 instance in `us-east-1b` and configure Elastic Load Balancing connection draining with `deregistration_delay.timeout_seconds` set to 30 so that in-flight requests complete before an instance is removed from service.
choices.explanation: Adding a single second instance in one additional AZ still leaves the web tier vulnerable to the failure of either of the two occupied AZs. Connection draining improves graceful deregistration but does not add fault tolerance across all three AZs.

choices.text: Configure Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached with a `num_cache_nodes` value of 3 and nodes distributed across all three AZs, using the ElastiCache auto-discovery endpoint so the application connects to all nodes for session data.
choices.explanation: Memcached does not replicate data between nodes; each node holds a distinct partition of the keyspace. If one node fails, its session data is permanently lost, causing active users on that node to lose their sessions. This does not eliminate the session cache as a single point of failure.

questions.tip: Focus on which configurations provide automatic failover managed by AWS rather than approaches that still require manual intervention after a failure.
questions.explanation:
Distributing the Auto Scaling group across all three AZs eliminates the web tier single point of failure. Enabling RDS Multi-AZ and ElastiCache for Redis with automatic failover eliminates the database and session cache single points of failure, all with minimal operational overhead because AWS manages the failover automatically.

**Why it works:** The `--vpc-zone-identifier` with three subnet IDs instructs Auto Scaling to balance instances across all AZs. RDS `--multi-az` creates a synchronous standby in a different AZ with automatic promotion. ElastiCache for Redis `--automatic-failover-enabled` with multi-AZ replicas promotes a replica automatically when the primary fails.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Option C: Manual snapshots provide disaster recovery, not high availability. Restoring from a snapshot requires manual effort and significant downtime, which does not eliminate a single point of failure.
- Option D: Adding one instance in a second AZ still leaves the architecture vulnerable to either AZ failing; using an Auto Scaling group spanning all three AZs with a minimum of 3 is the correct pattern.
- Option E: Memcached partitions data without replication, so any node failure permanently evicts that node's data. Session data loss does not constitute fault tolerance.

skills: 2.2.5: Implementing strategies to ensure the durability and availability of data (for example, backups).

choices.text: Create an AWS Backup resource assignment that tags the RDS instance and DynamoDB table with a shared tag (for example, `backup-policy=financial`) and configure the backup plan selection to match that tag.
choices.explanation: Resource assignments in AWS Backup use tag-based or ARN-based selection to associate resources with a plan. Without an assignment, the plan does not protect any resources.

choices.text: Enable automated backups on the RDS instance by setting `--backup-retention-period 35` and enable point-in-time recovery (PITR) on the DynamoDB table via `--point-in-time-recovery-specification PointInTimeRecoveryEnabled=true`.
choices.explanation: Enabling native service backups is separate from AWS Backup plans. These settings do not associate the resources with the centrally defined AWS Backup plan, leaving the team with two uncoordinated backup mechanisms.

choices.text: Attach an IAM policy granting `backup:StartBackupJob` to the `AWSBackupDefaultServiceRole` and specify the RDS and DynamoDB ARNs as `Resource` elements in the policy.
choices.explanation: The `AWSBackupDefaultServiceRole` already carries the permissions needed to back up supported services. Adding ARNs to the role policy does not link specific resources to the backup plan; that requires a resource assignment.

choices.text: Deploy the backup plan using `aws backup put-backup-plan` and then call `aws backup start-backup-job` with the `--resource-arn` parameter for each resource to manually trigger the first backup.
choices.explanation: Manually invoking `aws backup start-backup-job` creates one-off jobs rather than enrolling resources in the scheduled plan. This approach does not ensure ongoing automated coverage at the required RPO.

questions.tip: A backup plan on its own does not protect any resources until something links specific resources to that plan.
questions.explanation:
AWS Backup separates the backup plan (schedule, lifecycle, vault) from the resource selection (which resources are covered). A resource assignment -- defined by tag or ARN -- is required to associate resources with a plan.

**Why it works:** Using a shared tag and a tag-based resource assignment is the recommended approach for enforcing centralized backup policies across multiple services at scale. When both the RDS instance and the DynamoDB table carry the `backup-policy=financial` tag, the assignment automatically includes them in the hourly plan, satisfying the 1-hour RPO requirement.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Option B: Enabling native service backups (RDS automated backups, DynamoDB PITR) is independent of AWS Backup plans. It does not provide the centralized control the team requires and creates separate, unmanaged backup policies.
- Option C: The `AWSBackupDefaultServiceRole` already has the necessary permissions; modifying its policy does not enroll resources in the plan. Resource enrollment requires a resource assignment, not an IAM change.
- Option D: `aws backup start-backup-job` triggers ad-hoc jobs. It does not enroll resources in the scheduled plan and provides no ongoing protection aligned to the RPO.

skills: 2.2.5: Implementing strategies to ensure the durability and availability of data (for example, backups).
questions.question:
You are designing a data durability strategy for a healthcare company that stores patient records in Amazon S3 (versioning enabled) and appointment data in Amazon RDS for MySQL. Regulatory requirements mandate that all data must be recoverable to any point within the last 5 days, deleted objects in S3 must be recoverable for 90 days, and backup copies must exist in a second AWS Region. The company has no on-premises infrastructure.

Which TWO actions should the architect take to meet these requirements?

choices.text: Configure Amazon S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) on the source bucket with a replication rule that includes all objects, and add an S3 Lifecycle rule on the destination bucket to expire non-current versions after 90 days.
choices.explanation: CRR replicates new and existing objects to a second Region, satisfying the cross-Region copy requirement. Retaining non-current versions for 90 days ensures deleted objects remain recoverable for the mandated period.

choices.text: Enable AWS Backup with a plan that backs up the RDS instance every hour using a cross-Region copy rule targeting the secondary Region, with a retention period of at least 5 days.
choices.explanation: AWS Backup cross-Region copy rules duplicate RDS snapshots to a second Region automatically, satisfying both the point-in-time recovery requirement (5-day retention) and the cross-Region durability requirement for the database.

choices.text: Enable S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode on the source bucket with a 90-day retention period and disable versioning to prevent object modification.
choices.explanation: S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode prevents deletion but does not replicate data to a second Region. Disabling versioning would break point-in-time recovery and is incompatible with Object Lock requirements.

choices.text: Enable RDS automated backups with a `--backup-retention-period` of 5 days and configure Multi-AZ to replicate data synchronously to a standby instance in the same Region.
choices.explanation: Multi-AZ provides availability within a single Region but does not place backup copies in a second Region as required. Automated backups without a cross-Region copy rule also fail to meet the geographic durability mandate.

choices.text: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that triggers an AWS Lambda function nightly to copy S3 objects to a bucket in the second Region using `aws s3 sync`, and export RDS snapshots manually each week.
choices.explanation: A nightly `aws s3 sync` is not continuous replication and does not recover objects deleted between sync runs. Weekly manual RDS snapshot exports cannot support a 5-day point-in-time recovery window.

questions.tip: Consider which AWS-native features provide continuous, automated, cross-Region data copies for both object storage and relational databases.
questions.explanation:
Meeting both the 5-day point-in-time recovery requirement and the cross-Region copy requirement for two different storage layers requires purpose-built replication and backup features for each service.

**Why it works:** S3 CRR provides continuous, automatic object-level replication to a second Region, and non-current version lifecycle policies ensure deleted objects are retained for 90 days. AWS Backup cross-Region copy rules replicate RDS snapshots to a second Region on a defined schedule, satisfying both the RPO and geographic durability requirements for the database.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Option C: Object Lock prevents tampering but does not copy data to another Region. Disabling versioning would eliminate the delete-recovery capability the regulation requires.
- Option D: Multi-AZ is a single-Region availability feature and does not produce cross-Region backup copies. Automated backups alone do not satisfy the second-Region requirement.
- Option E: Nightly sync leaves gaps in recovery coverage for objects changed or deleted between runs. Weekly manual RDS exports cannot support a 5-day continuous recovery window.

skills: 2.2.6: Selecting an appropriate DR strategy to meet business requirements.
questions.question:
Management requires a DR strategy for a customer-facing e-commerce platform running on Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL and a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The recovery time objective (RTO) is 15 minutes and the recovery point objective (RPO) is 5 minutes. The platform must resume full production traffic in the secondary Region within the RTO. Budget constraints allow for some idle standby capacity but not a fully active duplicate environment.

Which DR strategy BEST meets these requirements?

choices.text: Implement a warm standby strategy: maintain a scaled-down but running EC2 Auto Scaling group and an RDS read replica in the secondary Region, promote the read replica to primary on failover, and update the Amazon Route 53 weighted routing policy to shift 100% of traffic to the secondary Region.
choices.explanation: Warm standby keeps infrastructure active at reduced scale, enabling promotion and scale-out within minutes. Promoting an RDS read replica and adjusting Route 53 routing satisfies a 15-minute RTO and 5-minute RPO without the cost of a fully active duplicate.

choices.text: Implement a pilot light strategy: replicate data continuously to an RDS read replica in the secondary Region, but leave EC2 instances stopped. On failover, start and configure the EC2 instances, promote the read replica, and update Route 53 to route traffic to the secondary Region.
choices.explanation: Pilot light minimises cost but typically requires 30-60 minutes to launch, configure, and validate EC2 instances after a failure event, which exceeds the 15-minute RTO requirement.

choices.text: Implement a backup-and-restore strategy: take hourly RDS snapshots and store AMI backups in the secondary Region. On failover, restore the RDS snapshot, launch EC2 instances from the AMIs, and update Route 53 to point to the new environment.
choices.explanation: Backup-and-restore typically yields RTOs measured in hours and RPOs equal to the snapshot interval (up to 1 hour), which does not meet the 15-minute RTO or 5-minute RPO.

choices.text: Implement a multi-site active/active strategy: deploy a full production stack in both Regions, use Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing to split traffic, and configure RDS Global Database for bidirectional replication.
choices.explanation: Active/active satisfies the RTO and RPO requirements but doubles infrastructure costs and complexity. With budget constraints explicitly excluding a fully active duplicate environment, this strategy does not meet the business requirements.

questions.tip: Match each DR strategy's typical RTO range against the stated requirement, and consider which strategies involve pre-provisioned but not fully scaled infrastructure.
questions.explanation:
Warm standby is the correct DR strategy when the RTO is measured in minutes and the RPO requires near-continuous replication, but a full active/active deployment is cost-prohibitive.

**Why it works:** A warm standby environment runs continuously at reduced capacity in the secondary Region. The RDS read replica is kept in near-real-time sync (satisfying the 5-minute RPO), and the small but running Auto Scaling group can scale out rapidly. Promoting the read replica and updating the Route 53 weighted policy are operations that complete well within 15 minutes.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Option B: Pilot light leaves compute stopped, requiring instance launch and configuration time after a failure. This pushes the realistic RTO beyond 15 minutes.
- Option C: Backup-and-restore involves restoring snapshots and relaunching entire environments, yielding RTOs of 1 hour or more and RPOs tied to the snapshot schedule.
- Option D: Active/active does meet the RTO/RPO but requires a fully active duplicate environment in both Regions at full scale, which the budget constraints explicitly prohibit.

skills: 2.2.6: Selecting an appropriate DR strategy to meet business requirements.
questions.question:
Following a production incident that caused 4 hours of downtime, a financial services company must redesign its DR architecture. The new requirements are: RTO of 10 minutes, RPO of 1 minute, failover must be automated with no manual DNS changes, and the solution must handle both EC2-based application servers and an Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster. The team has approved a budget for continuously running resources in the secondary Region.

Which TWO actions should the architect take to meet these requirements?

choices.text: Convert the Aurora MySQL cluster to an Aurora Global Database with a secondary Region cluster, and use the `aws rds failover-global-cluster` API to promote the secondary cluster, achieving a typical RPO of under 1 second.
choices.explanation: Aurora Global Database replicates with typically less than 1 second of lag, satisfying the 1-minute RPO. The `aws rds failover-global-cluster` managed failover API automates promotion of the secondary cluster.

choices.text: Configure Amazon Route 53 Application Recovery Controller (ARC) with a routing control that switches traffic to the secondary Region, and integrate the failover with an Amazon EventBridge rule to trigger the EC2 and Aurora failover steps automatically.
choices.explanation: Route 53 ARC routing controls provide reliable, automated DNS-layer failover without manual intervention. Combining ARC with EventBridge automation satisfies the no-manual-DNS-changes requirement and the 10-minute RTO.

choices.text: Deploy AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS) agents on the EC2 application servers to replicate data to the secondary Region, and configure DRS to launch recovery instances automatically on failover.
choices.explanation: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery is designed for server replication and meets the RTO/RPO requirements for EC2, but the question asks for two actions and this option does not address the Aurora database failover requirement, making it incomplete as a standalone choice for the combination.

choices.text: Enable automated backups on the Aurora cluster with a 1-day retention period, and use AWS Lambda to restore the latest snapshot in the secondary Region when a CloudWatch alarm detects primary Region failure.
choices.explanation: Restoring a snapshot takes 30-60 minutes and would not meet the 10-minute RTO. A 1-day retention period also does not guarantee a 1-minute RPO.

choices.text: Update the Amazon Route 53 simple routing record for the application endpoint to point to the secondary Region load balancer ARN, and rely on manual execution of a runbook to perform the switch during a failover event.
choices.explanation: Simple routing records require manual updates during failover, which violates the no-manual-DNS-changes requirement and cannot guarantee a 10-minute RTO when human intervention is required.

questions.tip: Consider which combination of services automates both the data-layer failover and the traffic-layer failover within the stated RTO and RPO.
questions.explanation:
Meeting a 1-minute RPO with automated failover for both Aurora and EC2 requires a continuously replicating database solution paired with an automated DNS failover mechanism.

**Why it works:** Aurora Global Database provides sub-second replication lag and a managed failover API, satisfying the 1-minute RPO for the database tier. Route 53 Application Recovery Controller provides health-check-driven, automated routing control changes that eliminate manual DNS steps and enable traffic cutover within the 10-minute RTO.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Option C: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS) is appropriate for EC2 server replication but the question is asking for two actions that together cover the full architecture. DRS does not address the Aurora failover requirement; Aurora Global Database and Route 53 ARC together form the complete solution.
- Option D: Snapshot-based restore cannot meet a 10-minute RTO or 1-minute RPO.
- Option E: Manual DNS changes violate the automation requirement and introduce unpredictable failover times.

skills: 2.2.7: Using AWS services that improve the reliability of legacy applications and applications not built for the cloud (for example, when application changes are not possible).
questions.question:
The organization is migrating a legacy monolithic application to AWS. The application runs on Windows Server and uses a hard-coded configuration file that binds it to a single static IP address for all inbound connections. The application binary cannot be modified. The operations team needs to improve availability so that traffic is automatically routed away from unhealthy instances without requiring code changes to the application.

Which solution improves availability without modifying the application?

choices.text: Place the EC2 instances running the legacy application behind a Network Load Balancer (NLB) with a static Elastic IP address assigned to the NLB, configure a TCP health check on the application port, and register the instances as NLB targets.
choices.explanation: An NLB with an Elastic IP satisfies the static IP requirement while providing automatic health-check-based traffic routing. No application code changes are needed; the NLB absorbs the connectivity layer.

choices.text: Assign a static Elastic IP address directly to each EC2 instance, configure Amazon Route 53 health checks against each instance IP, and use a Route 53 failover routing policy to shift traffic to the secondary instance on failure.
choices.explanation: Route 53 DNS failover introduces propagation delays (typically 60-300 seconds) during which the failed instance is still being used. Assigning individual Elastic IPs also does not provide load distribution across instances.

choices.text: Deploy an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in front of the instances, configure an HTTP health check on the application endpoint, and bind the application configuration to the ALB DNS name.
choices.explanation: The legacy application has a hard-coded static IP and cannot be modified to use a DNS name. An ALB provides a DNS name, not a static IP, and modifying the application configuration is stated as not possible.

choices.text: Configure an EC2 Auto Scaling group with a minimum of 2 instances and a lifecycle hook that replaces unhealthy instances, assigning the same Elastic IP to new instances via a `UserData` script on launch.
choices.explanation: Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks replace failed instances, but the Elastic IP reassignment via `UserData` introduces a gap between instance failure and IP reassignment. During this window, traffic is interrupted rather than automatically routed to a healthy instance.

questions.tip: Identify which load balancer type supports static IP addresses at the listener level, satisfying a hard-coded IP constraint without touching the application.
questions.explanation:
When a legacy application cannot be modified and requires a static IP, a Network Load Balancer with an Elastic IP is the correct AWS pattern.

**Why it works:** NLBs support static IP addresses (or Elastic IPs) per Availability Zone, which means the IP the application configuration references can remain fixed. The NLB performs TCP-level health checks and stops routing traffic to unhealthy targets automatically, improving availability without any application code change.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Option B: Route 53 failover is DNS-based and introduces TTL-dependent propagation delays, creating outage windows. It does not provide the seamless, sub-second traffic shifting of a load balancer.
- Option C: ALBs expose a DNS name, not a static IP. Because application changes are not possible, the hard-coded IP cannot be updated to a DNS name.
- Option D: Elastic IP reassignment via `UserData` requires the new instance to boot and run the reassignment script before traffic recovers, creating a recovery gap rather than eliminating it.

skills: 2.2.7: Using AWS services that improve the reliability of legacy applications and applications not built for the cloud (for example, when application changes are not possible).
questions.question:
After reviewing the architecture, the engineering team identifies two legacy components that need reliability improvements without application refactoring. The first is a batch processing application on EC2 that reads jobs directly from a shared network file system (NFS) and crashes if the NFS becomes temporarily unavailable, losing in-flight jobs. The second is a Windows IIS web application that has no retry logic and returns HTTP 502 errors to users when a single backend EC2 instance becomes overloaded. Neither application can be modified.

Which TWO actions should the architect take to improve reliability for these components?

choices.text: Replace the NFS-based job queue for the batch application with Amazon SQS, configure the batch workers to poll `sqs:ReceiveMessage` with visibility timeouts set longer than maximum job duration, and use dead-letter queues (`--redrive-policy`) to capture failed jobs.
choices.explanation: Amazon SQS decouples the batch workers from the job source, eliminating the single point of failure caused by NFS unavailability. Visibility timeouts prevent job loss when a worker crashes, and dead-letter queues capture jobs that repeatedly fail.

choices.text: Place the IIS web application instances in an EC2 Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer configured with a target group that uses HTTP health checks, and set the target group's slow start duration and deregistration delay to allow in-flight requests to complete before routing stops.
choices.explanation: An ALB distributes traffic across multiple healthy IIS instances, eliminating the single-instance overload condition. Health checks remove unhealthy instances automatically, and deregistration delay prevents connection drops during instance replacement, all without modifying the IIS application.

choices.text: Mount Amazon EFS on all batch worker EC2 instances as a replacement for the NFS share, and configure the application to read job files from the EFS mount point at `/mnt/efs/jobs`.
choices.explanation: Amazon EFS provides a managed, highly available file system, but simply replacing NFS with EFS does not protect in-flight jobs if the batch application crashes mid-processing. The fundamental problem -- job loss on crash -- requires a durable queue, not just a more reliable file system.

choices.text: Enable Amazon CloudWatch Application Insights on the IIS instances to detect HTTP 502 errors and trigger an Amazon EC2 instance reboot via AWS Systems Manager Run Command when error rates exceed a threshold.
choices.explanation: Rebooting an overloaded instance takes minutes and does not prevent 502 errors from reaching users during the reboot window. This approach treats symptoms rather than eliminating the single-instance capacity constraint.

choices.text: Configure an AWS Lambda function to periodically check the NFS share's availability using a custom Amazon CloudWatch metric and use an Amazon SNS notification to alert the operations team when NFS is unreachable.
choices.explanation: Alerting the operations team on NFS failures requires manual intervention and does not improve automated reliability. This approach does not prevent in-flight job loss or reduce the application's dependency on NFS availability.

questions.tip: Consider which AWS-managed services can absorb the failures that the legacy applications cannot handle themselves, without requiring changes to the application code.
questions.explanation:
Improving reliability for applications that cannot be modified requires placing AWS-managed resilience services in front of or behind those applications, absorbing failure modes the applications cannot handle.

**Why it works:** Amazon SQS with visibility timeouts and dead-letter queues transforms the fragile NFS-based job delivery into a durable, decoupled pattern -- jobs are not lost if workers crash because SQS retains unacknowledged messages. An ALB with Auto Scaling eliminates the single-instance overload point for the IIS application and routes traffic only to healthy instances, resolving the HTTP 502 errors without any code change.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Option C: EFS improves NFS availability but does not protect jobs that are in-flight when a worker process crashes. A durable queue is required to prevent job loss.
- Option D: Rebooting the overloaded instance adds downtime rather than preventing overload. Users still experience 502 errors during and after the reboot.
- Option E: Alerting on NFS failure requires manual intervention and does not automate recovery or prevent job loss.

skills: 2.2.8: Using purpose-built AWS services for workloads.
questions.question:
The engineering team needs to support a global gaming leaderboard that requires single-digit millisecond read and write latency for player score updates across three AWS Regions. The leaderboard data is small (under 10 GB), writes occur frequently from all Regions simultaneously, and the team must avoid managing replication logic in application code.

An architect proposes the following to create the table:

```cli
aws dynamodb create-table \
  --table-name GameLeaderboard \
  --attribute-definitions AttributeName=PlayerId,AttributeType=S \
  --key-schema AttributeName=PlayerId,KeyType=HASH \
  --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST \
  --region us-east-1
```

Which additional step completes the architecture to meet the multi-Region, low-latency requirement?

choices.text: Run `aws dynamodb create-global-table --global-table-name GameLeaderboard --replication-group RegionName=us-east-1 RegionName=eu-west-1 RegionName=ap-southeast-1` to enable DynamoDB Global Tables, which provides active-active multi-Region replication with sub-second propagation.
choices.explanation: DynamoDB Global Tables extends a table to multiple Regions with active-active writes and sub-second replication, satisfying the single-digit millisecond write latency and eliminating custom replication logic.

choices.text: Deploy an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster in each Region and configure the application to write leaderboard scores to ElastiCache using sorted sets (`ZADD`), with a background Lambda function replicating data between clusters every 30 seconds.
choices.explanation: ElastiCache Redis sorted sets offer sub-millisecond latency for leaderboard operations, but cross-Region replication requires custom Lambda logic, which the requirement explicitly prohibits. The 30-second sync interval also introduces inconsistency windows.

choices.text: Migrate the leaderboard to Amazon Aurora Global Database with a primary Region in `us-east-1` and read replicas in `eu-west-1` and `ap-southeast-1`, routing all write traffic to the primary Region endpoint.
choices.explanation: Aurora Global Database supports fast cross-Region reads but funnels all writes through a single primary Region. This introduces write latency for players in non-primary Regions and does not satisfy the simultaneous multi-Region write requirement.

choices.text: Enable DynamoDB Streams on the `GameLeaderboard` table and deploy an AWS Lambda function in each Region that reads stream records and writes updates to a local DynamoDB table replica, managing conflict resolution in the Lambda code.
choices.explanation: DynamoDB Streams with Lambda replication requires custom conflict resolution logic in application code, which directly violates the requirement to avoid managing replication logic. DynamoDB Global Tables provides this capability natively.

questions.tip: Identify which purpose-built AWS database feature provides active-active multi-Region writes without requiring custom replication code.
questions.explanation:
DynamoDB Global Tables is the purpose-built AWS service for active-active multi-Region workloads requiring low-latency writes from multiple Regions simultaneously.

**Why it works:** Global Tables uses a `create-global-table` API call to extend the existing DynamoDB table to additional Regions. AWS manages all replication internally with sub-second propagation and last-writer-wins conflict resolution. No application-level replication logic is required, and all Regions accept writes at single-digit millisecond latency.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Option B: ElastiCache Redis provides excellent leaderboard performance within a Region but requires custom cross-Region sync Lambda functions, violating the no-custom-replication requirement.
- Option C: Aurora Global Database is read-optimised for secondary Regions; writes must go to the primary Region, creating write latency for geographically distant players and contradicting the simultaneous multi-Region write requirement.
- Option D: DynamoDB Streams with Lambda replication is a valid DIY pattern but requires custom conflict resolution code, explicitly violating the requirement to avoid managing replication logic in application code.

skills: 2.2.8: Using purpose-built AWS services for workloads.
questions.question:
To meet a 99.99% SLA, a media streaming company needs to redesign two components of its platform. The first is a video upload pipeline where global content creators upload large video files (2-20 GB) directly to Amazon S3. Upload speeds from Asia-Pacific are poor because traffic traverses the public internet to a bucket in `us-east-1`. The second is a live event analytics component that receives 500,000 click and view events per second during peak events and currently drops records because the downstream processing database cannot keep up.

Which TWO purpose-built AWS services should the architect introduce to address these bottlenecks?

choices.text: Enable Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration on the upload bucket by setting `aws s3api put-bucket-accelerate-configuration --bucket media-uploads --accelerate-configuration Status=Enabled`, routing upload traffic through AWS edge locations to accelerate transfers from Asia-Pacific.
choices.explanation: S3 Transfer Acceleration routes uploads through the nearest AWS CloudFront edge location and then over the AWS backbone network to the destination bucket, significantly improving upload throughput for geographically distant users without any architecture changes.

choices.text: Replace the direct database writes for the analytics component with an Amazon Kinesis Data Streams stream, configure producers to publish events to the stream with `PutRecords`, and have downstream consumers read from the stream at a pace the database can sustain.
choices.explanation: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams is purpose-built for ingesting high-throughput event data (millions of records per second). It decouples producers from consumers, absorbs traffic spikes, and allows downstream consumers to process at a sustainable rate, eliminating record loss.

choices.text: Deploy an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the S3 upload bucket with an origin configured to `media-uploads.s3.amazonaws.com`, and instruct content creators to upload files to the CloudFront distribution URL.
choices.explanation: CloudFront is a content delivery network optimised for caching and distributing downloads, not uploads. CloudFront does not accelerate PUT operations to S3 origins; S3 Transfer Acceleration is the correct purpose-built service for upload acceleration.

choices.text: Place an AWS Global Accelerator in front of the S3 bucket's REST API endpoint to route upload traffic over the AWS backbone network, improving latency from Asia-Pacific by directing traffic to the nearest AWS edge location.
choices.explanation: AWS Global Accelerator improves TCP/UDP traffic routing for services like EC2, ALB, and NLB, but it does not support Amazon S3 as a backend endpoint. S3 Transfer Acceleration is the S3-native feature for global upload acceleration.

choices.text: Replace the analytics event writes with an Amazon SQS FIFO queue, configure producers to send events to the queue using `sqs:SendMessage`, and have a single consumer Lambda function poll the queue and batch-insert records into the database.
choices.explanation: SQS FIFO queues are limited to 3,000 messages per second per queue (with batching). At 500,000 events per second, a single FIFO queue would be immediately throttled. Kinesis Data Streams is purpose-built for this scale of streaming ingestion.

questions.tip: Select the AWS services specifically designed for the two distinct problems: accelerating large-object uploads from distributed global locations, and buffering very high-throughput event ingestion.
questions.explanation:
Each bottleneck requires a purpose-built AWS service matched to its specific scaling and performance characteristics.

**Why it works:** S3 Transfer Acceleration uses AWS edge infrastructure and the internal AWS network to dramatically improve upload performance from geographically distant locations, directly addressing the Asia-Pacific upload latency. Amazon Kinesis Data Streams is designed for high-throughput, real-time data ingestion at hundreds of thousands to millions of records per second, decoupling the ingest layer from downstream processing to eliminate record loss during peak events.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Option C: CloudFront caches and delivers content to end users; it does not accelerate S3 PUT (upload) operations. Uploads to a CloudFront URL would not be forwarded to S3.
- Option D: AWS Global Accelerator improves routing for ALB, NLB, and EC2 endpoints, but Amazon S3 is not a supported origin type for Global Accelerator.
- Option E: SQS FIFO queues are capped at 3,000 messages/second (high-throughput mode), far below the 500,000 events/second requirement. Standard SQS lacks ordering guarantees needed for analytics, and neither matches Kinesis's purpose-built streaming throughput.

skills: 3.1.2: Determining storage services that can scale to accommodate future needs.
questions.question:
The platform team is designing a media processing pipeline that will ingest user-uploaded video files and store them for downstream transcoding jobs. The dataset is expected to grow from 50 TB to several petabytes over three years as the user base expands globally. All processed files must remain immediately accessible via HTTPS, and the architecture must require no manual capacity provisioning as data volume grows.

Which storage service BEST meets these requirements?

choices.text: Store all files in Amazon S3 using the `s3:PutObject` API; configure a lifecycle policy to transition objects to `S3 Intelligent-Tiering` after 30 days.
choices.explanation: Amazon S3 scales to exabytes with no capacity management, serves objects over HTTPS natively, and `S3 Intelligent-Tiering` automatically optimises cost as access patterns change.

choices.text: Provision a 500 TB Amazon EFS file system in `General Purpose` mode and mount it on the transcoding EC2 fleet using the `nfs4` protocol.
choices.explanation: Amazon EFS does scale automatically, but it is a POSIX NFS file system optimised for shared file access from compute - not native HTTPS object access. It also incurs higher per-GB cost and is not designed for petabyte-scale object storage.

choices.text: Attach a 50 TB `io2` Amazon EBS volume to the primary processing instance and use EBS snapshots to archive older files.
choices.explanation: Amazon EBS volumes are bound to a single Availability Zone and a single instance at a time. Manual snapshot management is required for growth, and EBS does not expose an HTTPS object endpoint.

choices.text: Use Amazon S3 with a fixed `STANDARD` storage class and manually increase the bucket quota through a Service Quotas request each quarter.
choices.explanation: Amazon S3 bucket storage capacity is unlimited by default - there is no quota to increase. Choosing `STANDARD` exclusively and ignoring lifecycle policies does not invalidate scalability, but the framing of quarterly manual quota requests is factually incorrect and adds unnecessary operational overhead.

questions.tip: Think about which service requires zero capacity planning as data volume reaches petabyte scale.
questions.explanation:
Amazon S3 is an object store with virtually unlimited capacity that requires no pre-provisioning. Objects are accessed via HTTPS using the S3 REST API or pre-signed URLs.

**Why it works:** S3 scales automatically from bytes to exabytes. The `S3 Intelligent-Tiering` storage class monitors access patterns and moves objects between tiers without retrieval fees, making it well-suited to growing datasets with evolving access patterns. No administrator action is needed to accommodate growth.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Option B: Amazon EFS auto-scales its storage but is a network file system accessed via NFS - not an HTTPS object store. Per-GB cost is significantly higher than S3 at petabyte scale.
- Option C: Amazon EBS volumes require manual resizing, are attached to a single instance, and have no native HTTP access layer.
- Option D: The premise is flawed - S3 has no bucket capacity quota to request. The `STANDARD` class alone is not wrong for scalability, but the described manual process does not exist.

skills: 3.1.2: Determining storage services that can scale to accommodate future needs.
questions.question:
You are designing storage for a genomics research platform. Scientists upload large sequencing datasets (100 GB to 2 TB per run) several times per week. Active analysis jobs read these files intensively for the first 30 days, after which files are rarely accessed but must be retrievable within minutes when a cold case is reopened. The solution must scale to accommodate years of accumulated data without pre-provisioning capacity and must minimise ongoing storage cost.

Which TWO actions should the architect take?

choices.text: Store uploaded datasets in Amazon S3 with the `S3 Standard` storage class to support high-throughput reads during the active analysis window.
choices.explanation: `S3 Standard` delivers high availability and throughput for frequently accessed objects, making it appropriate for the 30-day active period without imposing minimum storage durations.

choices.text: Configure an S3 Lifecycle rule to transition objects to `S3 Standard-Infrequent Access` (`S3 Standard-IA`) after 30 days to reduce per-GB storage costs while retaining millisecond retrieval.
choices.explanation: `S3 Standard-IA` costs roughly 45% less per GB than `S3 Standard` and retrieves objects in milliseconds - satisfying the requirement for minute-scale retrieval of cold data.

choices.text: Provision a 500 TB Amazon EFS file system and mount it on analysis EC2 instances so that storage scales automatically without provisioning.
choices.explanation: Amazon EFS does scale automatically but charges approximately 10x the per-GB rate of `S3 Standard-IA`. For a dataset that accumulates over years and is mostly cold, EFS is cost-prohibitive and does not provide an HTTPS object interface.

choices.text: Transition objects to `S3 Glacier Deep Archive` after 30 days using a Lifecycle rule to achieve the lowest possible storage cost.
choices.explanation: `S3 Glacier Deep Archive` retrieval takes 12 hours for standard retrieval, which violates the requirement for minute-scale access to cold files.

choices.text: Deploy AWS Storage Gateway in `Volume Gateway` mode to present iSCSI volumes to analysis servers and archive snapshots to Amazon S3.
choices.explanation: Storage Gateway Volume mode is designed to extend on-premises storage to AWS. It does not provide a scalable cloud-native object store and adds unnecessary gateway infrastructure for a cloud-native workload.

questions.tip: Consider the two-phase access pattern and which storage class aligns to each phase without over-provisioning.
questions.explanation:
The workload has two clearly defined phases: intensive read access for 30 days followed by infrequent access with minute-scale retrieval SLA. Amazon S3 meets both phases through storage class tiering.

**Why it works:** `S3 Standard` handles the high-throughput active period with no retrieval fees. A Lifecycle transition to `S3 Standard-IA` after 30 days reduces per-GB cost by roughly 45% while still providing millisecond latency - satisfying the cold-retrieval SLA. Both classes scale infinitely without pre-provisioning.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Option C: Amazon EFS is far more expensive per GB and is optimised for shared POSIX file access, not large-scale archival.
- Option D: `S3 Glacier Deep Archive` retrieval latency (up to 12 hours) violates the minutes requirement.
- Option E: Storage Gateway Volume mode is an on-premises integration pattern and is not appropriate for a cloud-native research platform.

skills: 3.2.1: Decoupling workloads so that components can scale independently.
questions.question:
The engineering team needs to process customer order events generated by a front-end checkout service. The checkout service can burst to 5,000 events per second during flash sales, while the downstream inventory system can only safely process 200 events per second. The team wants to decouple the two systems so that each can scale independently without data loss during bursts. They run the following command to create the queue:

```cli
aws sqs create-queue --queue-name order-events --attributes VisibilityTimeout=300
```

Which additional architecture decision BEST decouples the components and absorbs traffic bursts?

choices.text: Have the checkout service publish messages to the SQS queue using `sqs:SendMessage`, and configure the inventory system to poll the queue with `sqs:ReceiveMessage` at its own sustainable rate.
choices.explanation: SQS acts as a buffer: the producer writes at burst rate while the consumer reads at its own pace. The queue absorbs the rate difference, preventing data loss and allowing independent scaling.

choices.text: Have the checkout service invoke the inventory Lambda function directly using `lambda:InvokeFunction` with `InvocationType=RequestResponse` to ensure synchronous processing.
choices.explanation: Direct synchronous invocation tightly couples the two components. If the inventory system is overwhelmed or slow, the checkout service blocks, and there is no buffering against burst traffic.

choices.text: Create an Amazon SNS topic and subscribe the inventory system directly using an HTTPS endpoint so that SNS fans out events in real time.
choices.explanation: SNS is a pub/sub fanout service, not a buffer. It delivers messages immediately to subscribers and does not persist messages if the subscriber is unavailable or cannot keep up with the delivery rate.

choices.text: Configure the checkout service to write events to an Amazon DynamoDB table with a `TTL` attribute set to 60 seconds, and have the inventory system use DynamoDB Streams to consume events.
choices.explanation: DynamoDB Streams can decouple reads from writes, but DynamoDB is not designed as a message queue. A 60-second TTL may expire records before the inventory system processes them during sustained bursts, risking data loss.

questions.tip: Consider which service was purpose-built to buffer messages between producers and consumers operating at different throughput rates.
questions.explanation:
Amazon SQS is a managed message queue that decouples producers from consumers. The producer writes at any rate; the queue stores messages durably until the consumer retrieves them at its own pace.

**Why it works:** The checkout service sends order events to the SQS queue via `sqs:SendMessage`. The inventory system polls via `sqs:ReceiveMessage` at 200 events/second. During a 5,000 events/second burst, messages queue up and are processed without loss once the burst subsides. The `VisibilityTimeout=300` ensures messages are not reprocessed while in flight.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Option B: `lambda:InvokeFunction` with `RequestResponse` creates tight synchronous coupling. No buffering occurs and the checkout service is blocked by inventory throughput limits.
- Option C: Amazon SNS does not buffer messages - if the subscriber cannot accept delivery, the message is lost or must rely on a dead-letter queue configuration.
- Option D: Using DynamoDB with TTL is an anti-pattern for event queuing. Short TTL values risk premature expiry, and DynamoDB Streams retain records for only 24 hours.

skills: 3.2.1: Decoupling workloads so that components can scale independently.
questions.question:
During a production incident review, the team identified that a monolithic order processing service becomes a bottleneck when order volume spikes. Payment validation, inventory reservation, and shipment scheduling all run sequentially in the same process. The team wants to refactor the architecture so that each of these three downstream functions can scale independently based on its own workload, while ensuring no order event is lost if any one downstream component fails.

Which TWO actions should the architect take?

choices.text: Publish each order event to an Amazon SNS topic, and create individual Amazon SQS Standard queues subscribed to that topic for payment validation, inventory reservation, and shipment scheduling.
choices.explanation: SNS fan-out to per-function SQS queues decouples all three consumers. Each queue buffers messages independently, so a failure in one consumer does not affect the others, and no event is lost.

choices.text: Configure a dead-letter queue (DLQ) for each SQS queue using the `RedrivePolicy` attribute with a `maxReceiveCount` of 3 so that unprocessed messages are retained after repeated failures.
choices.explanation: A DLQ captures messages that exceed the `maxReceiveCount` threshold, preventing data loss when a downstream component fails repeatedly. This satisfies the no-lost-event requirement.

choices.text: Replace the monolith with a single AWS Lambda function that calls all three downstream APIs synchronously and retries on failure using exponential backoff.
choices.explanation: A single Lambda function calling all three APIs synchronously preserves tight coupling. A failure in any one downstream call delays or blocks the others, and does not allow independent scaling.

choices.text: Use an Amazon Kinesis Data Stream with a single shard so that all three consumers read from the same stream partition in order.
choices.explanation: A single-shard Kinesis stream serialises all reads to one partition. Because all three consumers share one shard's throughput, they cannot scale independently, and a slow consumer affects stream retention for others.

choices.text: Enable Amazon SQS long polling on each queue by setting `WaitTimeSeconds=20` so that consumer functions receive messages with lower latency.
choices.explanation: Long polling reduces empty API responses and slightly lowers latency and cost, but it does not decouple components or prevent message loss. It is a minor operational optimisation, not an architectural decoupling mechanism.

questions.tip: Focus on how to isolate each downstream function's failure domain while guaranteeing message durability.
questions.explanation:
The SNS fan-out plus SQS pattern is the standard AWS approach to decoupling one-to-many event-driven workloads. Each downstream function gets its own queue, so it can scale and fail independently.

**Why it works:** Publishing to a single SNS topic and subscribing three separate SQS queues means each consumer reads from its own buffer. Adding a `RedrivePolicy` DLQ to each queue ensures that messages failing after `maxReceiveCount=3` attempts are moved to a DLQ rather than lost, satisfying the durability requirement.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Option C: A single synchronous Lambda function is still tightly coupled - it cannot scale the three functions independently and a downstream failure propagates to all.
- Option D: A single Kinesis shard limits total read throughput to 2 MB/s split across all consumers and does not provide per-consumer independent scaling or buffering.
- Option E: Long polling is a latency and cost optimisation for SQS consumers, not a decoupling or durability mechanism.

skills: 3.2.2: Identifying metrics and conditions to perform scaling actions.
questions.question:
The organization is migrating a customer-facing REST API from fixed-size EC2 instances to an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. Historical data shows CPU utilisation fluctuates unpredictably, but the team knows that response latency degrades when the average number of in-flight requests per instance exceeds 800. They want Auto Scaling to add or remove instances automatically to keep user experience consistent, without over-provisioning during quiet periods.

Which scaling configuration BEST meets this requirement?

choices.text: Configure a target tracking scaling policy using the `ALBRequestCountPerTarget` predefined metric with a target value of `800`, attached to the Auto Scaling group via the ALB target group ARN.
choices.explanation: `ALBRequestCountPerTarget` directly measures in-flight requests per instance. Target tracking continuously adjusts capacity to maintain the target value, scaling out before latency degrades and scaling in during low traffic.

choices.text: Create a step scaling policy triggered by a CloudWatch alarm on `CPUUtilization` with a threshold of 70%, adding 2 instances when the alarm breaches and removing 1 when it drops below 30%.
choices.explanation: CPU utilisation does not directly correlate to request-per-instance saturation for this workload. The team explicitly identified request count per target as the degradation signal, not CPU.

choices.text: Configure a scheduled scaling action to add 4 instances every weekday at 08:00 UTC and remove them at 20:00 UTC based on anticipated business hours traffic.
choices.explanation: Scheduled scaling acts on predicted time-based patterns, not actual real-time load. Unpredictable traffic fluctuations will not be handled adequately by a fixed schedule.

choices.text: Create a target tracking policy using the `ASGAverageCPUUtilization` predefined metric with a target of 50%, and set a `ScaleInCooldown` of 300 seconds.
choices.explanation: `ASGAverageCPUUtilization` tracks CPU, not request count. The team's data shows CPU is an unreliable indicator for this workload; using it as the scaling metric will not reliably prevent latency degradation when request rates are high.

questions.tip: Consider which CloudWatch metric most directly measures the condition the team identified as the cause of latency degradation.
questions.explanation:
When a team has identified a specific load metric that correlates to degraded user experience, that metric should drive the scaling policy. Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling's target tracking policies can use ALB-native metrics directly.

**Why it works:** `ALBRequestCountPerTarget` is a predefined metric in Auto Scaling target tracking that counts the average number of requests per registered target in the ALB target group. Setting the target to `800` means Auto Scaling continuously adds instances as the count approaches 800 and removes them as load decreases - keeping latency stable with minimal over-provisioning.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Option B: Step scaling on `CPUUtilization` reacts to a metric the team identified as unreliable for this workload. It also requires manual threshold tuning and does not adapt as smoothly as target tracking.
- Option C: Scheduled scaling does not respond to actual real-time request volumes and will under-provision or over-provision when traffic deviates from the schedule.
- Option D: `ASGAverageCPUUtilization` has the same problem as Option B - CPU does not represent the per-instance request saturation point.

skills: 3.2.2: Identifying metrics and conditions to perform scaling actions.
questions.question:
After reviewing the architecture of a video rendering farm, the team finds that rendering jobs are submitted in large batches every morning at 07:00 UTC when overnight export tasks complete. The Auto Scaling group currently uses a simple reactive step scaling policy on `CPUUtilization`, but instances take 8 minutes to boot and warm up. By the time new instances are healthy, the queue depth has already grown large and jobs are delayed. The team wants to scale out proactively and scale in cost-effectively during idle afternoons.

Which TWO actions should the architect take?

choices.text: Enable Predictive Scaling on the Auto Scaling group using the `ForecastAndScale` mode with `CPUUtilization` as the load metric so that instances are pre-launched before the 07:00 batch arrives.
choices.explanation: Predictive Scaling analyses historical CloudWatch data to forecast load and pre-provisions capacity ahead of recurring traffic patterns. `ForecastAndScale` mode both forecasts and automatically adjusts the group's desired capacity.

choices.text: Configure a target tracking scaling policy using the `SQSApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible` custom CloudWatch metric with a target value set to maintain a maximum queue depth that keeps job latency acceptable.
choices.explanation: A custom CloudWatch metric for SQS queue depth allows Auto Scaling to respond to the actual number of waiting jobs. Combining this reactive policy with Predictive Scaling provides both proactive and responsive capacity management.

choices.text: Reduce the `DefaultCooldown` of the Auto Scaling group to 30 seconds so that the step scaling policy can launch replacement instances more frequently after each scaling event.
choices.explanation: Reducing the cooldown period allows faster sequential scale-out, but does not address the core problem of reactive scaling with an 8-minute boot time. Instances will still lag behind the burst unless capacity is pre-launched.

choices.text: Create a CloudWatch alarm on `NetworkIn` with a threshold of 1 GB/s and attach a simple scaling policy to add 10 instances when the alarm fires.
choices.explanation: `NetworkIn` measures inbound network throughput, not rendering job queue depth or CPU demand. For a batch rendering workload, this metric does not reliably indicate when additional rendering capacity is needed.

choices.text: Set `InstanceWarmup` to 0 seconds on the target tracking policy so that newly launched instances are counted as contributing to the scaling metric immediately.
choices.explanation: Setting `InstanceWarmup` to 0 causes Auto Scaling to treat instances as healthy and in-service before they are actually ready, distorting the scaling metric and potentially triggering premature scale-in before real capacity is available.

questions.tip: Consider both how to get ahead of the predictable daily burst and how to maintain responsiveness to actual queue depth.
questions.explanation:
For workloads with both predictable recurring bursts and real-time queue depth as the key scaling signal, a combination of Predictive Scaling and a queue-depth-driven target tracking policy provides the most complete solution.

**Why it works:** Predictive Scaling in `ForecastAndScale` mode learns the 07:00 pattern and pre-launches instances before the burst arrives, eliminating the 8-minute warm-up lag. The SQS `ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible` target tracking policy handles any unexpected variation in job volume throughout the day, scaling in during idle afternoons and out if an unscheduled batch appears.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Option C: A shorter cooldown still relies on reactive step scaling. With an 8-minute instance warm-up, faster cooldown cannot compensate for the lag at burst start.
- Option D: `NetworkIn` is not a meaningful demand signal for a rendering workload and would trigger arbitrary scaling unrelated to job backlog.
- Option E: Setting `InstanceWarmup` to 0 pollutes the scaling metric by counting unready instances as healthy, which can suppress further scale-out and cause premature scale-in.

skills: 3.2.3: Selecting the appropriate compute options and features (for example, EC2 instance types) to meet business requirements.
questions.question:
To meet a 99.99% SLA for a genomics data analysis platform, the engineering team must run large-scale parallel processing jobs that perform dense matrix computations on datasets up to 1 TB in size. Each job runs for 4-6 hours, requires the highest available floating-point performance, and must complete within a predictable time window. The jobs run on a fixed schedule and steady-state cluster size has been established. Cost is secondary to performance predictability.

Which EC2 instance type family is MOST appropriate?

choices.text: Use `hpc7g` instances, which are purpose-built for compute-intensive HPC workloads with high-bandwidth `EFA` networking and up to 64 Graviton3E vCPUs per instance.
choices.explanation: `hpc7g` instances are AWS's purpose-built HPC family combining Graviton3E processors optimised for floating-point with Elastic Fabric Adapter networking, providing the highest floating-point throughput and predictable inter-node latency for tightly coupled parallel jobs.

choices.text: Use `r6i.32xlarge` instances, which offer up to 1,024 GiB of memory optimised for in-memory data processing of terabyte-scale datasets.
choices.explanation: `r6i` instances are memory-optimised for workloads like in-memory databases and real-time analytics. Dense matrix computation is CPU and floating-point bound, not memory-bandwidth bound alone, making memory-optimised instances a less targeted fit than compute-optimised HPC instances.

choices.text: Use `t3.2xlarge` instances with CPU credits in `unlimited` mode to absorb burst compute demand during peak matrix operations.
choices.explanation: `t3` instances are burstable general-purpose instances designed for workloads with low average CPU usage and occasional spikes. Sustained 4-6 hour heavy floating-point jobs will deplete CPU credits rapidly, resulting in throttled performance and unpredictable completion times.

choices.text: Use `m5.24xlarge` instances, which provide a balanced CPU-to-memory ratio suitable for general-purpose workloads including analytics.
choices.explanation: `m5` instances are general-purpose and appropriate for balanced workloads. For sustained high floating-point HPC jobs requiring maximum compute density and predictable performance, purpose-built HPC or compute-optimised families outperform general-purpose instances.

questions.tip: Think about which instance family is purpose-built for tightly coupled parallel scientific computing with predictable floating-point performance.
questions.explanation:
When sustained floating-point performance and predictable job completion are the primary requirements, purpose-built HPC instance families outperform general-purpose or memory-optimised alternatives.

**Why it works:** `hpc7g` instances use AWS Graviton3E processors that deliver up to 35% better floating-point performance per core than Graviton3. They include Elastic Fabric Adapter (`EFA`) networking, which provides ultra-low-latency MPI communication essential for tightly coupled parallel matrix workloads. Running a fixed-schedule cluster on Reserved Instances compounds cost efficiency without sacrificing performance.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Option B: `r6i` memory-optimised instances excel at in-memory databases; they are not tuned for floating-point throughput and cost more per compute unit than HPC families for this workload.
- Option C: `t3` burstable instances will throttle to baseline CPU after credits are exhausted, producing variable and degraded job completion times over a 4-6 hour window.
- Option D: `m5` general-purpose instances lack the floating-point specialisation and `EFA` networking of HPC families, resulting in lower sustained parallel compute throughput.

skills: 3.2.3: Selecting the appropriate compute options and features (for example, EC2 instance types) to meet business requirements.
questions.question:
Management requires a machine learning training platform to reduce EC2 compute costs by at least 60% compared to On-Demand pricing while still completing GPU training jobs within a business-day window. Training jobs are stateful - they use checkpointing to Amazon S3 every 30 minutes so they can resume after interruption. The platform must handle occasional Spot Instance interruptions gracefully and automatically resubmit interrupted jobs.

Which TWO actions should the architect take?

choices.text: Launch training jobs on EC2 Spot Instances using `p3.8xlarge` or `p3.16xlarge` instance types, specifying multiple instance types and Availability Zones in the Spot Fleet request to maximise capacity availability.
choices.explanation: EC2 Spot Instances offer up to 90% savings over On-Demand. Specifying multiple GPU instance types and AZs in a Spot Fleet diversifies the request pool, reducing the probability of simultaneous interruption across the fleet.

choices.text: Configure the Spot Fleet or Auto Scaling group with a Spot Instance interruption handler that detects the 2-minute warning via the EC2 instance metadata endpoint `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/spot/termination-time` and triggers a checkpoint save before termination.
choices.explanation: EC2 provides a 2-minute interruption notice accessible via instance metadata. Intercepting this signal allows the training job to save a final checkpoint to S3 before the instance is reclaimed, ensuring minimal work is lost when resubmitting.

choices.text: Purchase 3-year Standard Reserved Instances for `p3.8xlarge` to lock in a 60% discount and guarantee capacity for training jobs.
choices.explanation: 3-year Standard Reserved Instances do provide approximately 60% savings, but they require a large upfront commitment for capacity that may be idle between training runs. Spot Instances achieve similar or greater savings without a multi-year commitment and are more appropriate for interruptible batch workloads.

choices.text: Use `p3.2xlarge` On-Demand Instances with EC2 Auto Scaling to scale out to 20 instances during peak hours, relying on horizontal scale to reduce per-job cost.
choices.explanation: On-Demand Instances do not achieve a 60% cost reduction - they are the baseline price. Scaling out more On-Demand instances increases total cost rather than reducing per-unit cost.

choices.text: Enable EC2 Hibernate on all GPU training instances so that interrupted jobs resume from the exact in-memory state without needing S3 checkpoints.
choices.explanation: EC2 Hibernate is not supported on GPU instance families such as `p3`. Even where supported, Spot Interruption causes immediate termination and does not trigger a hibernate snapshot, so relying on hibernate instead of S3 checkpoints is not viable.

questions.tip: Consider which purchasing model achieves the cost target for interruptible jobs, and how to handle the 2-minute Spot interruption notice.
questions.explanation:
Spot Instances are the most cost-effective compute option for fault-tolerant batch workloads. Combined with proper interruption handling, they satisfy both the cost and resilience requirements.

**Why it works:** Spot Instances on GPU families like `p3` deliver savings of 60-90% versus On-Demand. Diversifying across multiple instance types and AZs in a Spot Fleet reduces the likelihood of capacity shortfalls. The 2-minute Spot interruption notice, available at the instance metadata endpoint `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/spot/termination-time`, gives jobs enough time to flush a checkpoint to S3 so they can resume from the last saved state when resubmitted.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Option C: 3-year Reserved Instances require upfront commitment for capacity that sits idle between jobs. Spot Instances are better suited to batch workloads and provide equal or greater savings without lock-in.
- Option D: On-Demand pricing is the baseline - scaling more On-Demand instances increases total cost and does not reduce per-instance pricing.
- Option E: EC2 Hibernate is not supported on `p3` GPU instances, and Spot termination does not invoke the hibernate path even on supported instance types.

skills: 3.2.4: Selecting the appropriate resource type and size (for example, the amount of Lambda memory) to meet business requirements.
questions.question:
The platform team is deploying an AWS Lambda function that resizes images uploaded to Amazon S3. During load testing they observe that with the default 128 MB memory setting the function takes an average of 4,200 ms per invocation. The team runs AWS Lambda Power Tuning and captures the following result:

```json
{
  "128": { "averageDuration": 4200, "averageCost": 0.0000070 },
  "512": { "averageDuration": 1050, "averageCost": 0.0000044 },
  "1024": { "averageDuration": 530, "averageCost": 0.0000044 },
  "1536": { "averageDuration": 480, "averageCost": 0.0000059 }
}
```

The team needs the LOWEST per-invocation cost while keeping average duration below 1,500 ms.

Which Lambda memory configuration should the team select?

choices.text: Set the Lambda function memory to `512` MB using `aws lambda update-function-configuration --function-name image-resizer --memory-size 512`.
choices.explanation: At 512 MB, the average duration drops to 1,050 ms (below the 1,500 ms requirement) and the per-invocation cost of $0.0000044 is the lowest in the dataset, matching the cost at 1,024 MB but using less vCPU.

choices.text: Set the Lambda function memory to `1024` MB to achieve the best balance between speed and cost.
choices.explanation: At 1,024 MB the per-invocation cost is identical to 512 MB ($0.0000044), but higher memory allocates more vCPU, which is unnecessary when 512 MB already meets the duration target. Both are equally cost-optimal, but 512 MB is the minimum configuration that satisfies both constraints.

choices.text: Keep the Lambda function memory at the default `128` MB to minimise the per-invocation memory cost.
choices.explanation: At 128 MB the per-invocation cost is $0.0000070, which is higher than both 512 MB and 1,024 MB configurations. Lambda charges are a product of GB-seconds; lower memory with much longer duration can exceed the cost of a higher-memory faster execution.

choices.text: Set the Lambda function memory to `1536` MB to achieve the fastest possible duration and stay within the latency budget.
choices.explanation: At 1,536 MB the per-invocation cost rises to $0.0000059, which is 34% more expensive than the 512 MB and 1,024 MB configurations. The additional vCPU provides only a marginal 50 ms improvement over 1,024 MB and does not meet the requirement for the lowest cost.

questions.tip: Lambda billing is based on GB-seconds. Consider both duration and memory allocation when comparing per-invocation costs.
questions.explanation:
AWS Lambda pricing is calculated as the product of memory allocated (in GB) and execution duration (in milliseconds). Increasing memory also increases allocated vCPU, which can reduce duration enough to lower total cost.

**Why it works:** The power tuning data shows that 512 MB achieves 1,050 ms duration - comfortably under the 1,500 ms threshold - at $0.0000044 per invocation, tied with 1,024 MB for the lowest cost. Selecting 512 MB satisfies both constraints with the minimum memory footprint.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Option B: 1,024 MB costs the same as 512 MB but allocates more vCPU than needed. The question asks for the lowest cost that meets the duration target, so 512 MB is the more precise answer.
- Option C: 128 MB costs $0.0000070, which is 59% more expensive than 512 MB despite using less memory, because the 4,200 ms duration dominates the GB-seconds calculation.
- Option D: 1,536 MB costs $0.0000059, which is more expensive than both 512 MB and 1,024 MB, and only saves 50 ms over 1,024 MB - well within the latency budget at higher cost.

skills: 3.2.4: Selecting the appropriate resource type and size (for example, the amount of Lambda memory) to meet business requirements.
questions.question:
Following a production incident, a payments team discovers that their AWS Lambda-based checkout API experiences cold starts of 3-5 seconds when traffic spikes at midnight UTC when promotional campaigns launch. The Lambda function connects to Amazon DynamoDB and initialises a cryptographic signing library during cold start. End-to-end latency must stay below 500 ms at p99 during bursts. The function currently uses 256 MB memory and executes in 180 ms when warm.

Which TWO actions should the architect take?

choices.text: Enable Provisioned Concurrency on the Lambda function alias and schedule it to pre-warm the required number of execution environments before midnight UTC using Application Auto Scaling with a scheduled action.
choices.explanation: Provisioned Concurrency keeps initialised execution environments ready, eliminating cold starts. Scheduling a scale-up action ahead of the known midnight burst ensures capacity is warm before traffic arrives.

choices.text: Increase the Lambda function memory from `256` MB to `1024` MB to allocate more vCPU and reduce the initialisation time of the cryptographic signing library during cold start.
choices.explanation: Lambda allocates vCPU proportionally to memory. Increasing memory from 256 MB to 1,024 MB quadruples the allocated vCPU, which can significantly reduce the CPU-bound initialisation time of the signing library during the `Init` phase.

choices.text: Configure a Lambda `Reserved Concurrency` limit of 500 to guarantee that 500 concurrent executions are always available for the checkout function.
choices.explanation: Reserved Concurrency limits the maximum concurrent executions for a function - it does not pre-warm execution environments. Setting a reserved concurrency limit does not prevent cold starts; it only caps concurrency and can throttle the function if demand exceeds the limit.

choices.text: Migrate the Lambda function to a container image and set the `PROVISIONED_CONCURRENCY` environment variable to enable automatic warm pool management.
choices.explanation: There is no `PROVISIONED_CONCURRENCY` environment variable that enables automatic warm pool management. Provisioned Concurrency must be configured explicitly via the Lambda API or console, and container image deployment does not inherently reduce cold start time for this function.

choices.text: Increase the Lambda function `timeout` setting from the default 3 seconds to 30 seconds so that cold start initialisation has more time to complete.
choices.explanation: The `timeout` setting controls the maximum allowed execution duration before Lambda forcibly terminates the function. Increasing the timeout does not reduce cold start duration - it only prevents the function from timing out. Cold starts still take 3-5 seconds regardless of the timeout value.

questions.tip: Consider how to eliminate cold starts proactively for a known traffic pattern, and how resource sizing affects initialisation speed.
questions.explanation:
For latency-sensitive functions with predictable burst patterns, Provisioned Concurrency combined with appropriate memory sizing addresses both the cold start root cause and the initialisation duration.

**Why it works:** Provisioned Concurrency pre-initialises execution environments so that the `Init` phase (including the cryptographic library load) completes before any request arrives. Scheduling the scale-up before midnight using Application Auto Scaling ensures warm environments are ready for the burst. Increasing memory to 1,024 MB allocates 4x more vCPU, directly reducing the CPU-bound signing library initialisation time during any remaining cold starts and improving warm execution speed.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Option C: Reserved Concurrency sets an upper bound on concurrent executions but does not pre-warm environments. It can actually cause throttling if demand exceeds the reserved limit.
- Option D: There is no Lambda environment variable that activates Provisioned Concurrency. The feature must be explicitly configured through the AWS API or console.
- Option E: The `timeout` setting only governs the maximum total execution duration. Cold start latency is part of the `Init` phase and is not affected by the timeout configuration.

skills: 3.3.1: Configuring read replicas to meet business requirements.
questions.question:
The platform team manages a production Amazon RDS for MySQL `db.r6g.2xlarge` instance in `us-east-1`. A reporting application in `eu-west-1` runs complex read-heavy analytical queries that are adding latency to the primary instance. The team runs the following command to investigate replication options:

